title: Illicit Gold
subtitle: The rush to cash in on the criminal shadows of El Dorado
line: Gold from the Amazon is dug by the poor, taxed by armed groups, laundered through a refining chokepoint, and sold into markets that cannot tell where it came from. No test on earth can determine where a bar was mined.
synopsis:
Gold has never been worth more, and almost none of it has to say where it came from. In the Amazon, that gap has become an industry. We follow a single trade from the mud it comes out of to the wedding ring it ends up on: the garimpeiro who mixes mercury with his bare hands and eats fish from the river he poisons, the armed groups who don't dig but sell the diesel and collect the tax, the airstrip no inspector visits, and the furnace where the crime quietly ends and a commodity begins.

Because that's the part nobody talks about. There is no test on earth that can determine where a bar of gold was mined. Once it's melted, everyone's gold is the same gold, and every person who handles it afterward is telling the truth. We trace what that buys: a cartel the United States calls a terrorist organization, a state that launders through its own central bank, a shipment of Iranian oil, a payment to Hezbollah, a coin sold by the U.S. Mint with an eagle stamped on it. And in a field in Colombia, we find a man with a gamma-ray detector pulling land mines out of a farm, because gold routes are worth protecting with explosives.

This isn't a story about gold. It's about what happens when a crime becomes a commodity, and who pays for it.

title: Chemical Cartels
subtitle: How fentanyl became a weapon of war
line: How fentanyl became a weapon of war: the precursor trade, the labs, the ports, and the street. Eleven short films, watchable now.
synopsis: The fentanyl supply chain from Chinese precursor companies through cartel labs in Mexico and Canada to North American streets, and the illicit financing that follows the drug every step of the way.

segments.title: American Fallout
segments.sub: How fentanyl became a weapon of war
transcript: What if the deadliest war in America isn't being fought overseas, but right here on our streets?
Across the country, a chemical weapon is claiming lives faster than any bullet. It's not launched by missiles or drones. It's packaged, shipped, and sold, one dose at a time.
That weapon is fentanyl.
The fentanyl trade has unleashed a humanitarian crisis: a synthetic storm of addiction, grief, and collapse.

From San Francisco's Tenderloin to Philadelphia's Kensington to the coal towns of West Virginia, and all across the United States and North America, the numbers tell the story: one American dies every seven minutes.
Border agents intercept nearly 98% of the illicit fentanyl crossing from Mexico. But the devastation proves that the remaining two percent is enough to poison an entire nation.
And while the southern border dominates headlines, few are asking a more uncomfortable question: what's happening to the north?
Canadian shipments account for less than one percent of total fentanyl seized in the U.S., yet whispers from ports, labs, and financial hubs suggest something deeper, quieter, and far more organized.

Because what we see on our streets is only the final act of a transnational operation, one that hijacks legitimate supply chains, weaponizes global commerce, and turns chemistry into asymmetrical mass destruction and human misery.
To understand today's fentanyl scourge and related crime convergence, we have to trace the trail back to its source, within the illicit economies of the criminal underworld and into the shadows.

segments.title: The Illicit Beachhead
transcript: What happens when a crisis is so devastating that a nation's communities become a beachhead for transnational organized crime?
We trace the chemical trail north, straight into Canada, a nation grappling with the fentanyl crisis, which has made communities like Vancouver's Downtown East Side critical frontlines.
While the overall numbers are smaller, deaths are proportional to the US.
On the streets of the Downtown East Side, the story is familiar. Fentanyl, failed decriminalization policies, and community devastation. But there is a story lurking in the illicit shadows.

Canada is increasingly serving as a hub of criminality and illicit trade, fentanyl production, and distribution of illicit goods, cementing its status as the North American beachhead for the shadow economies.
The human cost is horrific, and it is highly localized.

Since January 2016, Canada has recorded close to 50,000 apparent fentanyl toxicity deaths. In 2024, the majority of fatalities were highly concentrated, with 84% of accidental deaths occurring in just three provinces: British Columbia, Alberta, and Ontario.

At the center of this storm is Vancouver, specifically the Downtown Eastside. The city operates as a cartel-controlled drug distribution hub for Chinese-produced synthetic chemicals, and as a safe haven for money launderers.
To understand the North American fentanyl crisis, we must follow the chemical trail back to its source: China.

segments.title: The Invisible Source
transcript: What happens when the deadliest drug crisis in North America begins thousands of miles away in Asia, inside a legitimate global supply chain?
To understand the North American fentanyl crisis, we must follow the chemical trail back to its source: China.

China is the primary source of fentanyl precursors and pill presses in North America. These chemicals are exported primarily to Mexico or sent directly to Canadian labs, often hidden within international mail or express consignment operations.

Through numerous hearings and investigations, the U.S. Congress has spotlighted how the Chinese government has actively subsidized the export of fentanyl precursors, and has encouraged sanctions against China-based individuals and companies involved in the illegal fentanyl trade.

A cross-border joint investigation exposed a specific international smuggling operation centered in Wuhan, China. The firm, Hubei Amarvel Biotech, was central to a conspiracy to import fentanyl precursor chemicals into the US, according to the U.S. Department of Justice. U.S. Attorney Danielle Sassoon noted that they did so with callous disregard for the effect that such deadly chemicals would ultimately have in the United States.
This investigation confirms that the fentanyl epidemic is not just a drug crisis. It is a sophisticated, global manufacturing, smuggling, and money laundering operation, and possibly worse.

Chinese criminal networks continue to be not only the main suppliers of precursor chemicals for fentanyl and meth to the drug cartels in Mexico, Canada, and the United States, but are also financing other illicit activities across the Western Hemisphere, including laundering the cartels' dirty money.
The chemical pipeline often starts thousands of miles away in China, yet its product lands on our streets across North America.

The chemicals are made in Asia, but an army of Chinese criminal groups move them into North America, and when converged with other asymmetrical threats, help to expand illicit economies, fund malign operations, and do greater harm to many impacted communities.

segments.title: The Cartels
segments.sub: Mexico's role in the fentanyl supply chain
transcript: What happens when a nation caught in the crossfire becomes the crucible for the world's most dangerous synthetic drug?
If China supplies the chemicals, Mexico cooks the poison for greater profits.
The Mexican cartels are no longer just drug traffickers. They're chemists, logisticians, CEOs of illicit empires, and transnational power brokers.

Hidden in industrial zones and rural enclaves across Sinaloa, Michoacan, and Jalisco are thousands of clandestine labs, where fentanyl is synthesized using Chinese precursors. These labs operate under the control, or taxation, of major cartels like the Sinaloa Cartel and CJNG, the Cartel Jalisco Nueva Generacion.
These cartels don't just produce fentanyl. They manage supply chains, diversify revenue streams across industries, and build military-grade enforcement units, some rivaling local police.

The rise of synthetic drugs like fentanyl has revolutionized cartel economics. Compared to heroin or cocaine, fentanyl is cheaper to produce, easier to conceal, and far more deadly per gram. A single kilogram can be diluted into 500,000 lethal doses, generating tens of millions in revenue.
Cartels have even begun vertically integrating: sourcing precursors from Asia, producing fentanyl in Mexico, and distributing it through networks that reach deep inside North America, and beyond.

Cartel control extends beyond drug labs through infiltration of government structures and market penetration. Entire regions of Mexico function as parallel states, where criminal organizations govern, tax, and control territory. Cartels exploit corruption, impunity, and poverty, creating a system that is both invisible and fully integrated into global commerce.
In December 2016, the Canadian government lifted the visa requirement for Mexican nationals. Intelligence warned it would facilitate drug smugglers and foot soldiers, but Ottawa proceeded anyway.

As a result, Mexican cartels increased their market share across numerous criminal activities in Canada. Serious-crime flags tied to Mexican nationals jumped 89% in one year. Whistleblowers confirmed that over 400 members of Mexican cartels entered Canada, with many establishing permanent illicit operations.

Mexico has become the fulcrum of the fentanyl pipeline, not just a waypoint, but the engine room of a global shadow economy, as the cartels diversify into other sectors including energy, agriculture, mining of critical minerals, and tourism. To stop the synthetic storm, we must understand the ecosystem of criminality that enables it.

segments.title: The Leaky Port
transcript: What happens when the infrastructure built to power your economy becomes the very doorway traffickers use to flood it with poison?
Canada's infrastructure, designed for legitimate trade, is being weaponized against us. Nowhere is this clearer than at our major port complexes.

Criminal networks utilize sophisticated methods to exploit commercial and trade channels, particularly inter-modal transportation nodes and maritime shipping. Fentanyl precursors and pill presses arrive via container ships or air cargo, often mislabeled as legitimate goods.

The Canada Border Services Agency faces a monumental challenge, screening millions of containers daily. In 2024 alone, CBSA intercepted 25,600 kilograms of illegal drugs, including a 775% increase in fentanyl seizures from 2023.

The Port of Vancouver represents the front door for the illicit supply chain flowing into Western Canada. It is a key entry point, but it is also a departure point: Canada is shifting from an import nation to a production and export hub for synthetic opioids. Canada-produced fentanyl is trafficked out of Canada to places like Australia, New Zealand, and Asia via maritime routes.

The ports, once symbols of economic strength, are now vulnerable entry points for organized crime's illicit trade expansion. We must expose how traffickers are utilizing our own global shipping and trade arteries to pump the fentanyl poison across the globe.
The Port of Vancouver was built to bring the world to Canada. But the smartest cartels realized: why risk the border when you can build the factory right in the customer's backyard?

segments.title: The Lab Next Door
transcript: What happens when the cartel's next fentanyl lab isn't hidden in the mountains of Mexico, but in the house across the street?
The threat is no longer distant. Transnational criminal organizations are no longer just importing finished products; they are building manufacturing labs right here, in North America's suburbs.

Canada has transitioned from being primarily a conduit for imported fentanyl to a production and export hub for synthetic drugs, especially to the Oceania region. This domestic production surge has been noted since before 2020.

The Mexican cartels, specifically the Sinaloa and Jalisco New Generation Cartels, along with biker gangs and Asian triads, have expanded their influence to establish fentanyl and meth production operations in western Canada. These organizations have acquired the ability to manufacture illicit fentanyl in sophisticated laboratories across Canada.

These labs use pill presses, often imported from China, to produce counterfeit medications with deadly precision. This move towards industrial-scale fentanyl lab operations, particularly in British Columbia and Quebec, has been fueled by sophisticated Canadian wolfpack brokers.

This evolution signals a dangerous corporate-style organizational model by criminal networks. When the labs move into our neighborhoods, the line between international trafficking and local violence disappears.
The delivery system is automated, but the territory is still physical. And to control the streets, the cartels needed a local partner with muscle.

segments.title: The Parcel Pipeline
transcript: What if the most dangerous drugs in the world aren't smuggled in by trucks or boats, but arrive on your doorstep in an ordinary package?

Not all trafficking looks like what we see on the border. Fentanyl and its precursors are increasingly delivered via global mail systems, disguised as e-commerce shipments, nutritional supplements, or electronics.
This is the parcel pipeline, and it's hiding in plain sight.
Criminal organizations exploit express consignment hubs, FedEx, DHL, UPS, and international mail systems, to move small, high-potency shipments that are hard to detect, but deadly in volume.

From Wuhan to Winnipeg, Shenzhen to Chicago, these small packages are often routed through multiple countries to mask origin, relabeled multiple times, and dispersed through micro-distribution networks.

In 2024, U.S. Customs and Border Protection reported seizures of fentanyl in mail parcels spiking by over 200% compared to 2022. Canada's CBSA also flagged a surge in synthetic drugs arriving through express consignment operations, with some shipments containing enough powder to kill hundreds of thousands.

Why do traffickers love mail? It's fast. It's global. It blends into millions of legitimate shipments. And law enforcement is stretched thin: only a fraction of packages can be inspected, especially in high-volume hubs like Los Angeles, Vancouver, and Toronto.

Forget tunnels and truckloads. The next wave of trafficking is algorithmic, automated, and airborne. If we don't address the weaponization of global commerce and fulfillment systems, the fentanyl poison will keep arriving, one shipped box at a time.

segments.title: The Syndicates
transcript: What happens when more than 600 criminal organizations stop competing, and start collaborating?

The criminal underworld in Canada is not fragmented; it is an integrated ecosystem. Over 600 organized crime groups operate within Canadian borders and Indigenous First Nation territories, networked across 48 countries.

This unprecedented crime convergence involves key players collaborating at the strategic and operational level. The most powerful organizations include the Mexican cartels, Chinese triads, and Iranian crime groups, which interconnect strategically across Canada. They are joined by Eurasian mafias, Punjabi gangs, Canadian motorcycle gangs, and Aboriginal criminal groups.

The Sinaloa and Jalisco New Generation Cartel are the most dangerous transnational criminal organizations in North America. They control drug production and trafficking routes. This infiltration accelerated dramatically after the 2016 lifting of the Mexican visa requirement, which enabled over 400 cartel members to enter and establish operations freely in Canada. Asian triads and money laundering enablers help to wash tens of billions of dollars in illicit proceeds every year.

Local distribution is dominated by outlaw motorcycle gangs, with the Hells Angels being the most influential. They act as a critical intermediary, handling local distribution and enforcement within Canada, ensuring the product moves through urban and rural markets.

This ecosystem demonstrates that organized crime is adopting corporate-style models. They are using alliances to expand their illicit operations, forming a sophisticated North American criminal ecosystem.
They have the product and the power. Now, they need a place to wash the billions of dollars soaked in blood.

segments.title: Dirty Profits
transcript: What happens when the safest place to hide dirty money is inside the national economy itself?
Today, Canada is a financial safe haven and one of the weak links in the international financial system for bad actors.

Across Canada, criminal networks continue to profit handsomely from an array of illicit activities that are endangering the health and safety of its citizens, imperiling the country's national security, threatening global peace, and financing greater insecurity around the world through the criminality of Mexican cartels, Chinese triads, Iranian-backed illicit finance networks, and state-sponsored malign influence networks.
The greatest organized crime threat in Canada is money laundering.

Canada's Criminal Intelligence Service estimated that $45 billion to $113 billion was being laundered and fully integrated into Canada's economy annually. This includes proceeds from illegal drug trafficking, fraud, corruption, counterfeiting, and other crimes.
Criminals exploit legitimate sectors to clean their profits.

Casinos: money is laundered through high-stakes gambling transactions in British Columbia and Ontario casinos. In recent years there have been significant advancements mitigating the laundering through casinos in BC. And while progress is being made, the illicit finance activity has now moved into digital currency and online gaming globally.
Real estate: dirty money is funneled into high-value property purchases, particularly in Toronto and Vancouver, where criminals use luxury real estate to clean illicit profits.

Underground banking: Chinese underground banking systems are crucial for moving millions across borders for Mexican cartels and Asian syndicates, including through WeChat, social messaging, and e-payment systems.

As the Cullen Commission and numerous recent news reports have indicated, banks in provinces across Canada have helped to launder tens of billions of dollars over the years for drug cartels, terrorist financiers, kleptocrats, oligarchs, and other criminals and rogue syndicates.

Similarly, law enforcement agencies in Canada and the United States have found connections between government casinos in British Columbia, casinos in Macau and Las Vegas, and international drug traffickers. Even Canadian banks, operating retail branches on both sides of the border, are attractive to criminal networks because they reduce detection risk. In October 2024, Canada's TD Bank pleaded guilty and paid $3 billion in penalties to the U.S. Departments of the Treasury and Justice for laundering the dirty money of the Mexican drug cartels and other organized criminal networks.

Furthermore, law enforcement investigations and intelligence assessments have repeatedly implicated the WeChat platform as facilitating the movement of billions of dollars of the cartels' illicit drug proceeds by Chinese money laundering networks. The encrypted nature of WeChat allows narco-traffickers to coordinate discreetly, moving billions of dollars from the United States to China, and ultimately back to Mexico, where the majority of fentanyl is produced.
Money laundering in Canada is its national security Achilles heel. It fuels greater criminality and weaponizes its economy, allowing cartels to grow their dirty money empires.
While the money hides in skyscrapers, the physical smuggling routes are moving to the margins, exploiting ancient paths and vulnerable communities.

segments.title: Arctic Frontlines
transcript: What happens when North America's oldest trade routes become its newest war zones?

Criminal networks are masters at exploiting borders, especially complicated ones. And increasingly, they're targeting Indigenous territories, which are becoming the forgotten frontlines of a shadow war.
From the river corridors of the Great Lakes to the frozen Arctic north, we're watching something unsettling happen.
Take the Cornwall, Massena and Akwesasne corridor, where Ontario, Quebec, and New York meet. It's a complex border zone, and that complexity makes it vulnerable.
Traffickers move migrants and drugs south. Guns flow north. Organized crime groups even trade narcotics for illicit tobacco to finance their operations.
But this isn't just a southern border story.
As global powers rush toward the Arctic, chasing resources and new shipping routes, a security vacuum is opening in the High North.

Remote Indigenous communities are being hit hard by organized crime and an influx of synthetic drugs. Young people in these communities are absorbing the shock of an illicit trade designed to exploit the most vulnerable, creating generational trauma in places with the fewest resources to respond.
From the St. Lawrence River to the Arctic Ocean, historic waterways are being repurposed, not just for trade, but for illicit gain.
And while the geographic frontlines are expanding, the chemical frontier is evolving even faster.
The next wave isn't coming. It's already here.

segments.title: The Next Wave
segments.sub: Carfentanil and the illicit chemical pipeline
transcript: What happens when the next generation of synthetic opioids becomes even harder to detect, and exponentially more lethal?
One tiny bit of carfentanil, the size of a grain of rice, can kill an entire sports stadium. It is 100 times more potent than fentanyl.
Fentanyl was just the beginning. The next wave of synthetic threats is already here, driven by the global chemical pipeline that feeds North American labs.

Criminal networks have industrialized their operations. They are not just seeking restricted chemicals, but are shifting to more powerful precursors as drug cocktails. This sophisticated chemical delivery system is weaponizing North America's legitimate infrastructure.

Today's chemical cartels are creating a dynamic ecosystem of criminality that profits from increasing lethality. They prioritize profit over human life, pushing increasingly potent and lethal synthetic opioids into North America and beyond. The fentanyl pipelines are deadly.

Detection is extraordinarily difficult because trafficking and evasive methods are constantly evolving. Most fentanyl exports now move through microtraffickers using courier and mailing services to ship directly to consumers.

The fentanyl crisis is a sophisticated and very profitable cog in an expanding ecosystem of criminality. Unless North America can develop coordinated cross-border responses and drug prevention strategies, these criminal networks will continue to use our own infrastructure, and our weaknesses, against us.

But for the world's most powerful cartels, drugs are just one line of business. They have realized that the ultimate way to wash dirty money is to turn it into clean commodities. They are trading white powder for solid gold.
